card.say: While it's still unknown, the send button stays disabled for that transfer, so the user can't start it again. If they try, the app reuses the same client transfer ID, not a new one. turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Client (screens, ViewModel, repository) talks to the server ledger and a local cache; server owns the ledger and does each transfer in one transaction; local DB caches reads and saves the transfer intent with its client transfer ID before sending
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Transfer history and details in scope; cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars and B has 0"]
card.heard: back to the first transfer, user switches to account C while A's request is in flight
card.say: The danger is that A's old response lands while C is on screen. Then C's balance or history could show A's transfer. So I'd tag every request, cache write and callback with the account and a session generation. When a response comes back, the repository checks the session. If it's no longer current, it drops the response and doesn't write it to the local database.

card.then: Next: how the pending row and the session check work together on restart.

more: The pending row needs the same check. On restart, the repository reads only the rows for the signed-in account, so A's pending row is never shown or retried while C is signed in. A retry for A only happens when A signs in again.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app.
Candidate: They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination.
Candidate: Planning by hand took a lot of time.
Candidate: They had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together.
Candidate: The AI planner did that work for them.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for the AI trip planner, in a team of five.
Candidate: I owned the technical plan, the agent design and the core backend.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The app team's own screens and the product decisions stayed with product and the app team.
Candidate: One trade-off: streaming meant users saw day one before the whole plan was checked, so we agreed what to show while it was still being made.
Interviewer: On the AI trip planner, you said you wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan — which exact pieces did you build yourself versus the app team?
Candidate: I wrote the SSE reading on Android myself.
Candidate: That means the client that opens the stream, parses each event and hands the day cards to the UI.
Candidate: I also wrote the fallback on the app side, so a failed check shows a safe default instead of a broken screen.
Candidate: The app team owned the screens themselves, the layout and styling of the day cards and product cards.
Candidate: We agreed the response format together, so my code and their screens fit.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made was how the app reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The user enters a destination, budget and days, then taps plan.
Candidate: The app opens the SSE connection and reads each event as it arrives.
Candidate: Each event is parsed into a day card, and the cards go to the UI through StateFlow, so day one shows first.
Candidate: If a check fails, my fallback shows a safe default instead of a broken screen.
Candidate: The tap sends the request to the backend, and the app opens the SSE connection.
Candidate: Each event arrives as a small JSON chunk.
Candidate: I parse it off the main thread, build the day card, and post it to the UI through StateFlow.
Candidate: So the screen updates card by card, not all at once.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a day card that sometimes showed twice.
Candidate: It only happened on slow networks, so I couldn't reproduce it at first.
Candidate: I suspected the UI was collecting the stream twice.
Candidate: A log of each event id showed the same event arriving twice after a reconnect.
Candidate: So the real cause was the reconnect, not the UI.
Candidate: I fixed it by ignoring event ids I had already handled.
Candidate: I also added a cap on the stored ids, so the dedupe set can't grow without bound over a long session.
Candidate: And I'd test the reconnect case by cutting the network in the middle of a stream and checking that no card shows twice.

Interviewer: You said a log of each event id showed the same event arriving twice after a reconnect — how did you confirm the duplicate was coming from the reconnect itself and not, say, the server re-sending on its own?
Candidate: Two things pointed to the reconnect.
Candidate: First, the duplicate only appeared after the connection dropped and came back.
Candidate: Second, the two copies had the same event id, and the second one arrived right after the reconnect, not later on its own.
Candidate: So I checked the server side too: the server only resends when a client reconnects and asks for the stream again.
Candidate: It doesn't push the same event twice on a live connection.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had three options.
Candidate: First, dedupe on the client by event id.
Candidate: Second, ask the server to keep a cursor and resume from it.
Candidate: Third, just restart the whole plan on a reconnect.
Candidate: I picked the client dedupe because it was small and I could ship it myself.
Candidate: The cursor is the better long-term fix, but it needs a backend change and a new contract.
Candidate: Restarting the plan throws away cards the user already sees.
Candidate: After release, I checked two things.
Candidate: The duplicate-card reports stopped, and when I cut the network mid-stream myself, no card showed twice.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: This was the Debon release I mentioned earlier.
Candidate: I found the broken back button during testing, before the release.
Candidate: I told the project manager the same day, before I had checked every page.
Candidate: I gave two options: ship the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and test the rest in a rush.
Candidate: I recommended the first one.
Candidate: He decided, and he took my recommendation.
Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change shipped in the next release.

Interviewer: On the Debon release, when you recommended shipping the old pages, what risk were you willing to accept, and who watched the data afterward — plus what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: On the Debon release, the risk I accepted was the old pages.
Candidate: They were already live, so they were the safer choice.
Candidate: My change waited one more release, and that was the cost I was willing to take.
Candidate: For the data, the project manager owned the release decision.
Candidate: I watched the crash reports in Bugly myself, and QA watched the main flows.
Candidate: The signal to pause would be a crash or a broken back button on a main flow.
Candidate: If that showed up, I'd ask to roll back that release and fix it first.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design, a few questions.
Candidate: Is the balance held by us, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: What should work offline?
Candidate: Does that match what you want first?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and the flow between them.
Candidate: The client is the Android app: the balance and history screens, a ViewModel, and a repository.
Candidate: The repository is the only place that talks to the server and to the local database.
Candidate: The server owns the ledger.
Candidate: It checks and debits the payer and credits the payee in one database transaction, so a balance never goes negative.
Candidate: The local database also keeps a pending-transfer table with a status column, so on app restart the repository can resume or reconcile any transfer that was sent but never confirmed.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: A types 80 dollars to B and taps send.
Candidate: The app saves the intent with a client transfer ID, then calls the server.
Candidate: The server checks A has enough, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: A ends at 2000 cents and B at 8000 cents.
Candidate: The results screen shows success only from the server's record.

Candidate: If the same ID comes again with the same amount and recipient, it doesn't move money twice.
Candidate: It just returns the original transfer's status.
Candidate: If the amount or recipient is different, it rejects it as a conflict.

Interviewer: You said the app saves the intent with a client transfer ID before calling the server — what exactly gets written to the local pending-transfer table at that moment, and what status does it start in?
Candidate: The history screen reads only from the local database, so it shows the pending row straight away.
Candidate: It shows "Processing" while the status is pending, and "Unknown, checking" when a lookup found nothing.

Interviewer: Your flow has the server reply "Transfer status" and then "Results screen from server record," but if that reply is lost and Android kills the process, what does A see on reopening, given the pending row you wrote before the request? Please update your sequence diagram.

Candidate: The first one succeeds: A goes from 10000 to 2000 cents, and B goes from 0 to 8000 cents.
